title: Gottes Speise
source: Brüder Grimm, Kinder- und Hausmärchen, Band 2, 7. Auflage (Ausgabe letzter Hand), Dieterich, Göttingen 1857, KHM 205. Text from Wikisource („Gottes Speise (1857)“, twice proofread against the original). Fresh translation made directly from the German; 1857 spelling preserved exactly.
about: Two sisters — one rich and childless, the other a widow with five children and no bread left to give them — meet when the widow begs a crust and is turned away. Blood runs from the loaf her sister's husband is cutting at home; when he hurries to the widow's room he finds three of the children already dead of hunger and the mother praying with the last two in her arms, and within moments all five and their mother are gone.

sentences.t: Es waren einmal zwei Schwestern, die eine hatte keine Kinder und war reich, die andere hatte fünf Kinder und war eine Wittwe und war so arm, daß sie nicht mehr Brot genug hatte, sich und ihre Kinder zu sättigen.
sentences.l: There were once two sisters — the one had no children and was rich, the other had five children and was a widow and was so poor that she had no more bread enough to feed herself and her children.
sentences.i: There were once two sisters. The one had no children and was rich; the other had five children and was a widow, and so poor that she no longer had bread enough to feed herself and her children.
sentences.n: “Wittwe” is the 1857 spelling of “Witwe,” widow — the story's first stroke is that the poor sister lost her husband. “sich sättigen” is the reflexive of sättigen, to eat one's fill, to be sated; here in a chain of two datives, “sich und ihre Kinder … sättigen,” for herself and her children.

sentences.t: Da gieng sie in der Noth zu ihrer Schwester, und sprach „meine Kinder leiden mit mir den größten Hunger, du bist reich, gib mir einen Bissen Brot.“
sentences.l: Then she went in her distress to her sister, and said “my children are suffering the greatest hunger with me, you are rich, give me a bite of bread.”
sentences.i: So in her distress she went to her sister and said, “My children are suffering the greatest of hungers with me. You are rich — give me a bite of bread.”
sentences.n: “gieng” is the 1857 spelling of “ging” (past of gehen). “die Noth” is the 1857 spelling of “Not,” need, distress. “Bissen” is a bite, a morsel — the smallest quantity a person could beg for.

sentences.t: Die steinreiche war auch steinhart, sprach „ich habe selbst nichts in meinem Hause“ und wies die Arme mit bösen Worten fort.
sentences.l: The stone-rich woman was also stone-hard, said “I myself have nothing in my house” and turned the poor woman away with harsh words.
sentences.i: The stone-rich woman was stone-hard as well, said, “I myself have nothing in my house,” and turned the poor woman away with hard words.
sentences.n: The tale plays the two “stein-” compounds off each other in a single line: “steinreich” (stone-rich, ‘rolling in it’) and “steinhart” (stone-hard, unfeeling). “die Arme” here is the substantival adjective — the poor woman — not the plural of “Arm.”

sentences.t: Nach einiger Zeit kam der Mann der reichen Schwester heim, und wollte sich ein Stück Brot schneiden,
sentences.l: After some time the husband of the rich sister came home, and wanted to cut himself a piece of bread,
sentences.i: After a while the rich sister's husband came home and was about to cut himself a slice of bread,
sentences.n: “sich ein Stück Brot schneiden” — a dative of interest: to cut a piece of bread for oneself. German lays this out with a plain reflexive dative where English has to say “for himself.”

sentences.t: wie er aber den ersten Schnitt in den Laib that, floß das rothe Blut heraus.
sentences.l: but as he made the first cut into the loaf, the red blood flowed out.
sentences.i: but as he set the first cut into the loaf, the red blood flowed out.
sentences.n: “wie” here means ‘as, when.’ “that” is the 1857 spelling of “tat” (past of thun/tun). “rothe” is the 1857 spelling of “rote” (red, inflected). The wonder is stated as plainly as everything else — no marveling, no gloss.

sentences.t: Als die Frau das sah, erschrack sie und erzählte ihm was geschehen war.
sentences.l: When the woman saw that, she took fright and told him what had happened.
sentences.i: When his wife saw it, she took fright and told him what had happened.
sentences.n: “erschrack” is the 1857 spelling of “erschrak” (past of the intransitive erschrecken, to take fright — one is startled, one does not startle another). What she has already told him and what she keeps back is left implied.

sentences.t: Er eilte hin und wollte helfen, wie er aber in die Stube der Wittwe trat, so fand er sie betend;
sentences.l: He hurried over and wanted to help, but as he stepped into the widow's parlor, so he found her praying;
sentences.i: He hurried over meaning to help, but when he stepped into the widow's room, he found her at prayer;
sentences.n: “betend” is the present participle of beten, to pray — used adverbially/predicatively here (“fand er sie betend” = found her praying), as English uses the -ing form. “so” before “fand” is the resumptive “so” that a German main clause takes after an initial subordinate clause — untranslated in the natural English.

sentences.t: die beiden jüngsten Kinder hatte sie auf den Armen, die drei ältesten lagen da und waren gestorben.
sentences.l: the two youngest children she had in her arms, the three eldest lay there and had died.
sentences.i: the two youngest children she held in her arms; the three eldest lay there and had died.
sentences.n: German fronts the object (“die beiden jüngsten Kinder”) and puts the subject after the verb — a very ordinary word order in German that English cannot copy without sounding stilted. “die drei ältesten” is the substantival superlative — the three eldest.

sentences.t: Er bot ihr Speise an, aber sie antwortete „nach irdischer Speise verlangen wir nicht mehr;
sentences.l: He offered her food, but she answered “after earthly food we no longer crave;
sentences.i: He offered her food, but she answered, “We no longer crave earthly food;
sentences.n: “Speise” is food, fare, sustenance — deliberately plain, not a specific dish. “irdischer” is the strong feminine dative singular of “irdisch,” earthly — “nach irdischer Speise” = for earthly food (“verlangen nach” + dative = to long for).

sentences.t: drei hat Gott schon gesättigt, unser Flehen wird er auch erhören.“
sentences.l: three has God already sated, our pleading he will also hear.”
sentences.i: God has already fed three of them; our pleading he will hear as well.”
sentences.n: “Flehen” is the nominalized infinitive of flehen, to plead, to entreat — pleading as a thing done. “erhören” is the verb reserved for a prayer or a plea being granted (Gebete erhören, ein Flehen erhören); “hören” alone would only be to hear the sound of it.

sentences.t: Kaum hatte sie diese Worte ausgesprochen, so thaten die beiden Kleinen ihren letzten Athemzug, und darauf brach ihr auch das Herz und sie sank todt nieder.
sentences.l: Scarcely had she uttered these words, when the two little ones did their last breath, and thereupon her heart also broke and she sank down dead.
sentences.i: Scarcely had she spoken these words when the two little ones drew their last breath, and thereupon her heart too broke, and she sank down dead.
sentences.n: “Athemzug” is the 1857 spelling of “Atemzug,” a drawing of breath — “den letzten Athemzug thun” is the fixed idiom for drawing one's last breath. “brach ihr … das Herz” is the dative of possession — literally ‘the heart broke to her,’ which is how German owns the body part in a clause like this. “todt” is the 1857 spelling of “tot” (dead).

glossary.arm: arm — poor, destitute (adjective; „war so arm“ = was so poor)
glossary.armen: der Arm — arms (dat. pl. Armen; „auf den Armen“ = in her arms)
glossary.verlangen: verlangen — to long for, to crave (verb; „verlangen nach“ + dat.; „verlangen wir nicht mehr“ = we crave no more)
glossary.wies: weisen — turned, showed (3rd sg. preterite; here with fort: „wies … fort“ = turned away, sent away)
